why_trail.why: The defect is exactly as diagnosed and the enumeration is mine, not inherited: four filesystem writes in the module, two of them unguarded and both inside _log, whose single call site at :461 sits outside run_engine's try/except. _log_rejection at :472-499 is the shape to copy -- OSError only, stderr, every occurrence, no batching. The regression test must drive a real server subprocess, because the crash presents to a client only as a closed connection; tests/test_mcp_friction_capture.py's McpRpcClient is the harness pattern to reuse, and its rpc() already raises on a missing reply.

Guarded each telemetry write separately rather than wrapping _log's body once: the call log and the start marker are two independent side-channels, and one destination being unwritable must not suppress the other -- the third test pins exactly that (call log writable, marker not). The catch is OSError, not bare Exception, so a programming error in this module still surfaces instead of hiding behind a telemetry message. The report goes through one new helper, _report_dropped_telemetry, copying _log_rejection's shape: stderr, flushed, every occurrence, the lost record carried in the message. The test asserts against the PARSED lost record, not the sentence around it -- my first draft grepped stderr for 'spine_status' and failed green-side, because the door logs the ENGINE verb 'current', not the tool name. That was a real reading: the record is the engine's, not the tool surface's.

The probe that killed the server at a69bbac4 now returns EXIT 0 with an answered call. The answer is isError:true naming the missing spine file -- the engine's own truth, surfaced instead of a dead process; fail-closed wording for that case is g3's lane, not mine. Two telemetry-drop reports on stderr, two stdout lines, both JSON-RPC 2.0, zero non-protocol lines. That last measurement matters because the pure-stdout test alone cannot discriminate: pre-fix stdout is EMPTY, which is trivially pure.

Two evidence defects of my own, both caught by reading output instead of intent, both now fixed and both recorded in the result rather than quietly repaired. First: 'git checkout -- <path>' restores from HEAD, and once the fix was committed HEAD WAS the fix -- so a re-measurement reported 7 passed under a header claiming the unfixed tree. Redone against b9135f1b explicitly with a grep-c assertion. Second: that same command stages what it restores, so the following 'commit --amend' silently dropped the source fix out of the commit; caught by reading 'git show HEAD:scripts/mcp_spine_server.py' rather than trusting the amend. Third, smaller: I claimed the existing start-marker test defended the separate guards. It does not -- a shared guard passes it -- so I added the test that does and proved it by mutation. The pattern under all three: a claim about the world verified against the world, not against what I meant to do.

amendments.reason: My own check text asserted a status line shape the skill's IMPLEMENTER_RESULT template does not use. The template writes '## Return status' with the bare value beneath it; my regex demanded '**Return status:** <value>'. Satisfying both would put the same value in the artifact twice, which is the drift the one-name-per-thing rule exists to prevent. Same intent, same strictness -- the value must still be exactly one of the five, lowercase -- read from the template's own shape.
